opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to start from what reasoning actually is. To me, reasoning is the ability to take a problem you can't solve in one step, break it into intermediate steps, and use those steps to reach an answer you couldn't have produced directly. So the question is what medium those intermediate steps live in.

With textual reasoning, the medium is language. Language is a highly compressed, abstract, symbolic system that humans built over thousands of years. When a model writes out a chain of thought, it's using concepts we've already distilled: numbers, logical connectives, names for things. That's why text reasoning has advanced so quickly. The pretraining data is full of human reasoning traces, and reinforcement learning can sharpen that ability very efficiently. Math, coding, and logic puzzles all fit naturally into that space.

Visual reasoning is different in a fundamental way. A lot of what we do when we reason about the physical world isn't really verbal. If you imagine rotating a chair to fit it through a door, or picture where a ball will land, or mentally fold a piece of paper, you're not narrating it to yourself in words. You're simulating something spatial and continuous. That information is very hard to compress into language without losing what matters. If you try to describe a complex geometric configuration in pure text, it gets long, awkward, and error-prone, while a single sketch makes it obvious.

So one way I'd put it: textual reasoning operates over abstractions humans have already created, while visual reasoning has to operate closer to raw perception, and often has to construct its own intermediate representations. That's much harder. Today many multimodal models still convert the image into text-like tokens and then do essentially textual reasoning. They "see" once and then "think in words." That works for some tasks, but it's not what people do. When we solve a geometry problem, we draw auxiliary lines, look again, revise. The visual medium is part of the thinking loop, not just the input.

From an intelligence perspective, I think both matter, and real general intelligence probably requires both and the ability to move between them. Language gives you abstraction and communication. Visual and spatial reasoning ground you in the world, which matters for embodied agents and robotics, things I care a lot about. A robot can't reason about grasping an object purely through text. It needs some internal model of geometry and physics.

The honest answer is that we're still early on visual reasoning. We don't yet have a clean equivalent of chain-of-thought for images, something where the model generates visual intermediate steps and RL makes them reliably useful. Some people are trying with image generation inside the reasoning loop, or with world models, but I think it's an open problem and one of the more interesting frontiers right now.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes textual reasoning, which operates through language and abstractions, from visual reasoning, which operates on spatial and visual information, and says both matter to intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't draw a hard line between them, and the longer I work on this the less I believe the line is real. What we call "textual reasoning" is reasoning that happens to be serialized into tokens, and what we call "visual reasoning" is reasoning over a representation that's spatial and continuous. But the underlying operation, in both cases, is building a model of some situation and then manipulating that model to reach a conclusion that wasn't explicitly given to you.

Where they do feel different is in what the representation makes cheap and what it makes expensive. Language is extremely good at abstraction and compression. I can say "the cup is to the left of the book," and I've thrown away almost everything about the scene except the one relation I care about. That's exactly why chain-of-thought works so well: you can carry a long argument step by step without having to hold the whole world in your head. The cost is that language is lossy. If you ask me whether the cup would fall if I tilted the table, text alone doesn't give me the geometry. I have to reconstruct it.

Visual reasoning is the opposite trade. The representation is dense, so a lot of the inference is almost free. You look at the table and you just see that the cup is near the edge. Nobody has to tell you. But that density makes it hard to do long, compositional chains. It's difficult to "think ten steps ahead" purely in pictures. You tend to externalize it, sketch something, move things around, and look again.

From a reinforcement learning perspective, which is where I come from, the thing I care most about is that the agent has to act in the world, and the world is not made of text. So when I look at a model that reasons well in language but poorly about space, I don't think it has learned a different kind of intelligence. I think it has learned a good internal language and hasn't yet grounded it. The interesting research question for me is not "which modality is the real reasoning," but how you get a system to translate fluently between the two, so that it can use text when it needs abstraction and use something closer to perception when it needs precision. Humans do this constantly without noticing. We're very far from that in machines, and I think most of the gap is on the grounding side, not the language side.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes textual and visual reasoning by their representations and tradeoffs, but explicitly says they are not separate kinds of intelligence and describes them as the same underlying operation. It does not present them as two distinct components of intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is partly about how information is represented. In textual reasoning, you’re working with information that has already been expressed as words and concepts. You can state a premise, make an inference, and describe the next step. Language gives you a convenient way to organize that process.

With visual reasoning, you often have to figure out the relevant structure first: what the objects are, how they relate spatially, and what might happen if something moves. Imagine rotating an object in your head. You may be able to predict what it will look like without describing every intermediate step in words.

But I wouldn’t treat these as completely separate kinds of intelligence. You can use language to help solve a visual problem, and you can use a mental picture to solve a problem presented in text. The interesting question is how a system moves between those representations—whether it can choose the representation that makes the problem easier, while preserving the relationships that matter.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes textual reasoning, which works with words and concepts, from visual reasoning, which identifies spatial structure and predicts visual changes. Its caveat that they can interact does not erase that distinction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is less about two separate kinds of intelligence and more about the representations you reason over. With text, someone has already organized the world into words and concepts. You’re reasoning over a description, and that description makes some information explicit while leaving other information out.

With vision, you have to figure out what the relevant things are in the first place: objects, relationships, motion, spatial structure. If you look at a table and ask whether a cup might fall, you need to understand its position relative to the edge, perhaps its balance, and what could happen next. You don’t necessarily need to translate all of that into sentences.

But the boundary is blurry. Language can support spatial reasoning, and visual reasoning can use concepts learned through language. To me, the interesting question is whether a system can build a useful representation, manipulate it, and draw conclusions that generalize. Text and images give us different ways to test that ability.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reasoning over text from reasoning over visual information, but frames them as different representations for one broader ability and explicitly rejects treating them as two separate kinds of intelligence. It does not clearly present them as two distinct components of intelligence.
